blocks.text: An infant with a floppy tone, an enlarged heart and muscle full of glycogen-laden vacuoles has no problem making ATP in her mitochondria; her problem lies in the acidic organelle that should recycle glycogen. Three small organelles, mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes, divide up energy production, degradation and oxidative detoxification.

blocks.markdown: Eukaryotic cells partition metabolism into organelles with specialised membranes, pH and enzymes. This unit covers **mitochondria** (ATP and apoptosis), **lysosomes** (digestion of material from endocytosis and autophagy) and **peroxisomes** (oxidative reactions).

blocks.title: Core definitions
blocks.text: A mitochondrion is a double-membrane organelle whose inner membrane carries the electron transport chain and ATP synthase and which generates most cellular ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. A lysosome is an acidic (about pH 4.5-5) membrane-bound organelle with acid hydrolases. A peroxisome is a single-membrane organelle that oxidises very-long-chain fatty acids and other substrates, producing hydrogen peroxide that its enzyme catalase breaks down.

blocks.markdown: **ATP production.** Electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass along the electron transport chain in the inner membrane, and the energy released pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. This builds a **proton-motive force** with an electrical part (the membrane potential $\Delta\psi$, about 150-180 mV, negative inside the matrix) and a chemical pH part. Protons return to the matrix through **ATP synthase**, driving phosphorylation of ADP. The electrical work to move one mole of ions of charge $z$ across a potential $\Delta\psi$ is $\Delta G = zF\Delta\psi$, with $F = 96485$ C per mol.

blocks.caption: Electrical free-energy change for moving a mole of ions of charge z across a membrane potential of Δψ (volts); F = 96485 C per mol

blocks.title: Why mitochondria can make ATP
blocks.prompt: Explain how a proton gradient across the inner membrane drives ATP synthesis, and predict the effect of an uncoupler that makes the membrane leaky to protons.

steps.text: Electron transport pumps protons from matrix to intermembrane space, storing energy as a gradient.
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, which couples this downhill flow to ADP phosphorylation.
An uncoupler lets protons bypass ATP synthase, so the gradient collapses, ATP production falls and the energy is dissipated as heat while the chain keeps running.

blocks.answer: ATP synthase harnesses the proton gradient; an uncoupler dissipates it, lowering ATP output and releasing heat.

blocks.markdown: **Apoptosis.** Mitochondria control the intrinsic pathway. Cell stress activates pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins (BAX and BAK), which permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane (an event called MOMP), while BCL-2 itself restrains this. **Cytochrome c** leaks from the intermembrane space into the cytosol and binds Apaf-1 to form the **apoptosome**, which activates **caspase-9**. Caspase-9 activates executioner **caspases** such as caspase-3, which dismantle the cell in an orderly way, without inflammation, unlike necrosis.

**Lysosomes.** The lysosomal membrane pumps protons inward, so the lumen is acidic, which activates acid hydrolases and keeps them inactive if they leak into the neutral cytosol (about pH 7.2). pH is $-\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]$, so each pH unit is a ten-fold change. Cargo arrives by **endocytosis** (and phagocytosis), where endosomes or phagosomes mature and fuse with lysosomes, and by **autophagy**, where a double-membrane **autophagosome** engulfs the cell's own organelles (mitophagy is the selective removal of mitochondria) and fuses with a lysosome. Products are recycled to the cytosol.

rows: Neurons; infant neurodegeneration with a cherry-red macular spot

blocks.title: Relating a disease to its enzyme
blocks.prompt: A baby has hepatosplenomegaly and macrophages that look like crumpled tissue paper. Which enzyme is deficient and what accumulates?

steps.text: Macrophages that cannot digest a lipid substrate become engorged: this is the Gaucher cell.
The substrate is glucocerebroside, normally degraded by glucocerebrosidase in lysosomes.
Because macrophages of liver, spleen and marrow are overloaded, the organs enlarge.

blocks.answer: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency with glucocerebroside accumulation (Gaucher disease).

blocks.markdown: **Peroxisomes.** Peroxisomes oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids (shortening them for further use), and their oxidases generate hydrogen peroxide, which **catalase** converts to water and oxygen. Failure of peroxisome function, such as in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, allows very-long-chain fatty acids to accumulate.

items: Mitochondria: oxidative phosphorylation (proton gradient, ATP synthase) and intrinsic apoptosis (cytochrome c, apoptosome, caspases).
Lysosomes: acidic digestion of endocytosed and autophagic cargo; one missing hydrolase causes a storage disease.
Peroxisomes: very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation and hydrogen peroxide removal by catalase.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Lysosomes and peroxisomes are both small enzyme-filled vesicles, but lysosomes are acidic digestive compartments, whereas peroxisomes carry out oxidation and detoxify hydrogen peroxide. Apoptosis is orderly and caspase-dependent, not the same as necrosis.

points: Mitochondria make ATP by oxidative phosphorylation using a proton gradient and trigger apoptosis through cytochrome c release, apoptosome formation and caspases.
Lysosomes digest cargo delivered by endocytosis and autophagy in an acidic lumen; storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs, Gaucher and Pompe arise from specific hydrolase deficiencies.
Peroxisomes oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids and use catalase to remove hydrogen peroxide.

questions.stem: A toxin makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons without blocking the electron transport chain. What is the expected result?

options.text: Oxygen consumption continues but ATP production falls and heat is released
Oxygen consumption stops and ATP rises
ATP synthase runs faster because the gradient is larger
Cytochrome c is immediately degraded in lysosomes

questions.correctOptionText: Oxygen consumption continues but ATP production falls and heat is released

distractorRationale.b: ATP does not rise without a gradient.
distractorRationale.c: The gradient is dissipated, not enlarged.

questions.explanation: Protons leak back without passing through ATP synthase, so the gradient collapses. The chain keeps oxidising fuel, but the energy is lost as heat rather than stored in ATP.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the intrinsic apoptotic pathway?

options.text: BAX/BAK permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane, cytochrome c is released, the apoptosome activates caspase-9, and executioner caspases dismantle the cell
Caspase-3 releases cytochrome c, which then permeabilises the nucleus, and BAX then activates the apoptosome
Lysosomes release hydrolases that digest the nucleus, then mitochondria release ATP
BCL-2 permeabilises the outer membrane and promotes cytochrome c release

questions.correctOptionText: BAX/BAK permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane, cytochrome c is released, the apoptosome activates caspase-9, and executioner caspases dismantle the cell

distractorRationale.c: This describes uncontrolled lysis, not apoptosis.

questions.explanation: Stress activates BAX and BAK, which permeabilise the outer membrane and release cytochrome c. Cytochrome c with Apaf-1 forms the apoptosome that activates caspase-9, which in turn activates caspase-3 for orderly dismantling.

questions.stem: A hepatocyte encloses an aged mitochondrion in a double-membrane vesicle that then fuses with a lysosome. What is this process?
questions.explanation: Autophagy delivers the cell's own components to lysosomes in autophagosomes. Mitophagy is the selective version for mitochondria.

questions.stem: A baby has an enlarged liver and spleen, bone pain, and macrophages with crumpled tissue-paper cytoplasm. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

distractorRationale.b: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease.
distractorRationale.c: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causes Pompe disease.

questions.explanation: Glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages that lack glucocerebrosidase, giving Gaucher cells and organ enlargement. Each storage disease is tied to one lysosomal enzyme.

questions.stem: An infant has cardiomegaly, hypotonia and muscle biopsies showing lysosomes packed with glycogen. Which enzyme deficiency explains this?

distractorRationale.d: The accumulation here is lysosomal, not cytosolic.

questions.explanation: Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase degrades glycogen taken into lysosomes; without it, glycogen accumulates there, particularly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. This is Pompe disease.

questions.stem: A lysosome has a luminal pH of 4.7 and the cytosol has a pH of 7.2. By what factor is the hydrogen ion concentration higher in the lysosome than in the cytosol? Give a dimensionless factor.
questions.explanation: pH is the negative log of [H+], so the difference of 2.5 pH units gives 10^2.5, about 316-fold. This steep gradient is why acid hydrolases are active in the lysosome and largely inactive if they leak into the cytosol.

questions.stem: The inner mitochondrial membrane potential is 160 mV (negative inside). Using delta G = zF delta psi with F = 96485 C per mol, calculate the electrical free energy released when 3 moles of protons (z = +1) move down this potential into the matrix, in kilojoules. Ignore the pH component.
questions.explanation: Electrical work per mole of protons is 96485 x 0.160 = 15.44 kJ. For 3 moles it is 46.3 kJ, comparable to the energy needed to phosphorylate a mole of ADP, which illustrates how a few protons moving through ATP synthase can drive ATP formation.

questions.stem: Explain how mitochondria produce ATP and how they trigger apoptosis.
markingGuide: Electron transport chain pumps protons into the intermembrane space, forming a proton gradient and membrane potential.
Protons flow through ATP synthase, driving ADP phosphorylation.
In apoptosis, BAX/BAK permeabilise the outer membrane and cytochrome c is released.
Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome with Apaf-1, activating caspase-9 and then executioner caspases.
Caspases dismantle the cell in an orderly manner, unlike necrosis.
questions.explanation: A full answer covers both functions mechanistically: the proton gradient for ATP and the cytochrome c to caspase sequence for apoptosis.

questions.stem: An infant has progressive neurodegeneration and a cherry-red macular spot. Explain how a deficiency of hexosaminidase A causes this picture, referring to the lysosome, the substrate and the affected cells.
markingGuide: Hexosaminidase A is a lysosomal hydrolase degrading GM2 ganglioside.
Deficiency means the substrate cannot be degraded and accumulates in lysosomes.
Neurons are rich in gangliosides, so they swell and are damaged, causing neurodegeneration.
Names a link between missing enzyme and lysosomal storage rather than failed synthesis.
questions.explanation: A single missing hydrolase blocks a degradative pathway. The substrate builds up in the cells that handle most of it, here neurons.

questions.stem: A few lysosomes rupture and release acid hydrolases into the cytosol, yet the cell is not digested. What explains this?

options.text: The hydrolases work best at acidic pH and are largely inactive at the cytosolic pH of about 7.2
The hydrolases are destroyed by catalase
The hydrolases are immediately pumped back by ATP synthase

questions.correctOptionText: The hydrolases work best at acidic pH and are largely inactive at the cytosolic pH of about 7.2

distractorRationale.b: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide, not hydrolases.

questions.explanation: Acid hydrolases have a pH optimum near 5, so they are much less active in the neutral cytosol. This provides a safeguard against uncontrolled digestion.
